claims.text: An integrated framework can independently model DFT-based electronic transport and machine-learning-based phonon transport in HfNbTaTiZr.
Calibrating the framework for defects and oxygen impurities will improve its predictions for oxygen-containing HfNbTaTiZr.
The new framework will reduce thermal-conductivity prediction error from approximately 30% to approximately 10%.
Accurately separating lattice and electronic heat-transport contributions is the reason the proposed framework will outperform earlier approaches.
The target material is bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
HfNbTaTiZr has significant atomic-scale lattice distortions.
HfNbTaTiZr exhibits significant variations in interatomic force constants.
Below 200 K, the lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are comparable.
Measurements on oxygen-containing HfNbTaTiZr span 300–1200 K.
Oxygen impurities induce atomic-scale lattice distortions and defect scattering in HfNbTaTiZr.
Oxygen-induced defects affect force-constant variations and mass disorder in HfNbTaTiZr.
Impurity and lattice disorder scatter electrons and alter electronic transport.
Mass disorder and force-constant variations scatter phonons in HfNbTaTiZr.
Independent calibration of electronic and phonon transport will improve the combined prediction of total thermal conductivity.
At 300–1200 K, the predicted total thermal conductivity will match an experimental range of approximately 10–17 W/(K m).
Existing approaches typically have thermal-conductivity errors near 30%.

Earlier approaches rely on simplified Debye-temperature-based analytical models or defect-free-crystal simulations and fail to separate electronic and lattice transport in oxygen-containing HfNbTaTiZr.
The predictions are restricted to bulk HfNbTaTiZr with roughly 1 wt.% oxygen at temperatures below 200 K and from 300 to 1200 K.
Magnetic-field modulation can separately resolve lattice and electronic thermal conductivity below 200 K for the proposed samples.
The hypothesis is falsified if predictions do not attain approximately 10% error or if predicted high-temperature conductivity lies outside 10–17 W/(K m).
